0.name: Population
0.description: Residents per km² of land. Each municipality's population (INE Padrón, 2025) is shared among its hexes in proportion to the part of the municipality each one covers. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

1.name: Income
1.description: Mean net income per person of each hex's municipalities, weighted by population (INE Household Income Distribution Atlas, 2024: tax records matched to the Padrón). It is a mean per person, not the US map's median per household. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

2.name: Poverty
2.unit: population below 60% of the median income
2.description: Share of residents whose income per consumption unit is below 60% of the national median, the EU at-risk-of-poverty threshold (INE Household Income Distribution Atlas, 2024: income from tax records, modified OECD scale). It is a threshold relative to Spain's income, not the US map's fixed poverty line. Population-weighted in hexes with several municipalities. Small municipalities may have no figure (statistical confidentiality) and do not count in their hex. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

3.name: Mean age
3.description: Mean age of the residents of each hex's municipalities, weighted by population (demographic indicators of the INE Household Income Distribution Atlas, 2024, drawn from the Annual Population Census). It is the mean: INE publishes no median age by municipality, which is what the US map shows. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

4.name: Born abroad
4.description: Share of residents born outside Spain (INE Annual Population Census, table 65031, 1 January 2026), population-weighted in hexes with several municipalities. It counts the place of birth, not nationality: a Spaniard born abroad counts; a foreigner born in Spain does not. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

5.name: Higher education
5.description: Share of residents aged 15 or over whose highest completed level of education is higher education: university degrees and higher vocational training (INE Annual Population Census, table 66592, 1 January 2024), weighted by population. The US map counts adults aged 25 or over with a bachelor's degree; INE gives age only for municipalities of 500 residents or more, so here everyone from 15 is counted and the share comes out lower. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

6.name: Homeowners
6.description: Share of main dwellings (a household's usual residence) that are owned, against renting and other forms of tenure such as rent-free use (INE Population and Housing Census, 1 January 2021: indicators by census section added up by municipality), weighted by population. The smallest municipalities have no figure: INE does not publish their sections (statistical confidentiality). Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

7.name: Home value
7.description: Mean value per built m² of free-market housing from the appraisals of Q2 2026 (appraised value statistic of the Ministerio de Vivienda; Spain: 2,355 €/m²). The figure is the province's, because the series by municipality cannot be downloaded: a hex carries its province's, or the population-weighted mean if it touches two. It is a price per m², not the US map's median value of a whole home. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

8.name: Heritage
8.description: Bienes de Interés Cultural (Spain's highest heritage protection: monuments, sites, historic ensembles) in each hex, as Wikidata places them. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

9.name: Museums
9.description: Museums in each hex: the 2,517 museums, galleries, science museums and interpretation centres of Spain that Wikidata places. Hover a hex to see their names. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

10.name: Designations of origin
10.description: How many of the 398 names Spain has in the EU register (eAmbrosia: PDO, PGI, wines and spirit drinks) include each hex in their area. 292 areas are those of the Ministry of Agriculture (2017 revision). For 92 the Ministry has not mapped (nearly all the PGI wines and the names registered since 2017) the area is the one their specification or EU single document delimits, drawn on the IGN's municipal boundaries; the tooltip says so after the kind: “community”, “province”, “island” or “municipalities” (a municipality only partly inside counts whole). The 14 single-estate wines without a Ministry area are an estate: they go on one hex, that of their municipality's centre (“estate”). Each hex lists the smallest areas first. Left off the map as no longer registered: Aceite de la Comunitat Valenciana (PDO), Carne Morucha de Salamanca (PGI). Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

11.name: Regional dishes
11.unit: dishes and products of the province
11.description: The 577 dishes, cured meats, cheeses, sweets, breads and wines that the Spanish Wikipedia lists under each province's cuisine (and that Wikidata classes as food or drink). Hover a hex to see its province's. Volunteer-edited: some provinces are far better covered than others. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

12.name: Pre-Roman peoples
12.description: The ancient people whose location in Pleiades is nearest each hex (up to 175 km): Vaccaei, Vascones, Cantabri, Ilergetes… and, in the south and east, the regions named after their peoples (Turdetania, Bastetania, Contestania). The borders are nearest-point territories drawn by this map: Pleiades gives each people a point, not a boundary. The names are in Latin or Greek, as in Pleiades.

13.name: Languages
13.description: Where each language is official, municipality by municipality, according to the law: co-official in all of Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, Galicia and the Basque Country; Aranese in the Val d'Aran; the Basque-speaking and mixed areas of Navarre (Ley Foral 18/1986); in the Valencian Community, the Spanish-speaking municipalities of Llei 4/1983 (where Valencian is co-official too); Asturian, protected but not co-official. Aragonese and the Catalan of Aragon have no published list of municipalities yet, so Aragon shows Spanish only. Dialects (Andalusian, Canarian…) are not legal categories and are not mapped.

14.name: Blue Flag
14.description: The 677 Blue Flag beaches of 2026-27, with name and municipality on hover. ADEAC gives each beach's municipality, not its position: 604 are in place because Wikidata or OpenStreetMap has a beach of that name in that municipality; the other 73 are shared among their municipality's coastal hexes.

15.name: Tourist dwellings
15.description: Dwellings let to tourists per 1,000 inhabitants: the 341,001 that INE finds advertised on the large platforms and matches to the Cadastre (experimental statistic, 05/2026), over the Padrón residents (2025). In a hex, the population-weighted mean of its municipalities. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

16.name: Fiestas of tourist interest
16.description: The 90 Fiestas of International Tourist Interest and the 164 of National Tourist Interest declared by the Secretaría de Estado de Turismo (Sanfermines, Fallas, the Tomatina, El Rocío, Holy Week in Seville…) and the 1,042 that 15 autonomous communities declare of regional tourist interest, each under its own name (Fiesta de Interés Turístico de Andalucía, Festa de Interese Turístico de Galicia…), each fiesta on the hex of its municipality's capital; a route or a valley, on those of all its municipalities, once per hex. A promoted fiesta counts once, at its highest category. With no municipality in their source (declared for a whole community or held in a different place each year), these are on no hex: «semana Santa de Andalucía», «Carnaval Hurdano». Hover a hex to see their names.

17.name: Bars
17.description: Bars and pubs in OpenStreetMap (amenity=bar and amenity=pub, 42,122 in Spain; no cafés or restaurants) per 1,000 Padrón inhabitants, counted in their municipality. In a hex, the population-weighted mean of its municipalities. Volunteers map them and coverage is very uneven: cities and tourist coasts are far better mapped than villages, where a zero can be an unmapped bar. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

18.name: Party index
18.description: This map's own index, not an official statistic: how many times Spain's usual a hex has in bars, tourist dwellings and fiestas of tourist interest, as the geometric mean of three factors. Bars and tourist dwellings: their number per inhabitant ÷ Spain's, counting each hex with 1,000 more residents at Spain's rate, so a hamlet with one bar does not pass for Benidorm. Fiestas: 1 + their points (International 2, National 1, regional 0.5). 1 is the usual; everything up to it stays dark.

19.name: Castles
19.description: The 3,009 castles of Spain that Wikidata places (alcazabas, alcázares, tower houses and ruined castles included; demolished ones left out). Hover a hex to see their names. Volunteer-edited: the coverage is not that of an official inventory. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

20.name: Bullrings
20.description: The 650 bullrings of Spain that Wikidata places (of any category; demolished ones left out). Hover a hex to see their names. Volunteer-edited: the coverage is not that of the official register.

21.name: Forest
21.description: Share of the hex's land covered by broadleaved, coniferous or mixed forest (CORINE 311–313). Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

22.name: Farmland
22.description: Share of the hex's land in crops, meadows or dehesas (CORINE 2xx, matched to NLCD classes 81 and 82). Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

23.name: Built-up
23.description: Share of the hex's land that is built up: urban fabric, industrial and commercial areas, transport networks, ports, airports and construction sites (CORINE 111, 112, 121–124 and 133; urban green and sports areas are not counted). Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

24.name: Broadband
24.unit: households covered at 100 Mbps or more
24.description: Share of each municipality's households that a fixed or fixed-wireless network of 100 Mbps or more reaches under peak demand (coverage report of the Ministerio para la Transformación Digital, June 2025, from the operators' data by cadastral parcel; Spain: 97.9%). It is coverage, not subscriptions: the US map counts subscribing households. A hex shows the population-weighted mean of its municipalities. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

25.name: Work elsewhere
25.unit: employed who work in another municipality
25.description: Share of employed residents who work in a municipality other than their own (in their province, in another province of their autonomous community or in another community), among those whose place of work is known (INE Annual Population Census, 1 January 2024; Spain: 57.3%). The 151 municipalities INE publishes (provincial capitals and main cities) have their own figure; the others take the rest of their province's (the province minus those municipalities). INE does not publish commuting time by municipality: this is where people work, not the US map's minutes to work. A hex shows the population-weighted mean of its municipalities. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

26.name: Religious weddings
26.note: Spain has no census of religion: this measures how people marry, not what they believe.
26.description: Share of the marriages of 2025 celebrated by a religious denomination (INE does not separate Catholic from other weddings in these tables), by the couple's place of residence (INE Marriage Statistics; Spain: 16.1%). The 150 municipalities INE publishes (provincial capitals and main cities) have their own figure; the others take the rest of their province's (the province minus those municipalities). A hex shows the population-weighted mean of its municipalities. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

27.name: Wildfires
27.note: Area burnt, not damage: land that burns twice counts twice.
27.description: Hectares burnt in each hex in the fires of 2016 to 2025 that the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS, Copernicus) mapped from satellite images: their perimeter, woodland or farmland, added up year by year (Spain: 1,284,332 ha in 7,303 fires). It records fires of about 30 ha or more (since 2021, with Sentinel-2, many smaller ones too); the smallest, which the ministry's statistic (EGIF) does count, are missing. It takes the place of the US map's FEMA disaster declarations. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

28.name: Life expectancy
28.description: Life expectancy at birth, both sexes, in 2024 (INE Basic Demographic Indicators). The 155 municipalities INE calculates it for have their own; the others take their province's, which includes those municipalities (a life expectancy cannot be subtracted). It takes the place of the US map's wellbeing index (CDC health estimates). A hex shows the population-weighted mean of its municipalities. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

29.name: Oldest old
29.unit: aged 85 and over among those 65 and over
29.note: It counts where people live: a care home raises its municipality's. Depopulation moves it less than the share of people over 65.
29.description: Oldest-old index: residents aged 85 and over per 100 aged 65 and over (INE Annual Population Census, 1 January 2026, provisional; Spain: 15.6%, 1,625,139 of 10,438,474). Some sources use 80 and over. It measures how long those who reach old age live, not how many old people there are: a village that loses its young rises in the share over 65, not in this index. A hex adds up the old residents of its municipalities, each by the share of its residents in the hex, before dividing, so a small village never counts alone. INE publishes every municipality, with no cell hidden. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

30.name: Centenarians
30.note: They are few: each hex counts 10,000 more residents at Spain's rate so a hamlet with one centenarian does not come first.
30.description: Residents aged 100 and over per 10,000 (INE Annual Population Census, 1 January 2026, provisional; Spain: 3.66, 18,164 centenarians). A hex adds up the centenarians and residents of its municipalities, each by the share of its residents in the hex, then moves towards Spain's rate as if it had 10,000 more residents at that rate: (centenarians + 10,000 × Spain) ÷ (residents + 10,000). Hover a hex to see each municipality with centenarians, with its whole count and its unsmoothed rate: a large municipality repeats its count in each of its hexes. Colours span the 2nd–98th percentile of hexes; values beyond are drawn at the end colours.

32.name: Longevity zones
32.note: This map's own index, not an official statistic. It leans on rural, ageing Spain.
32.description: How many of three measures a hex has at the top: oldest old (85+ ÷ 65+) of 16.8%, centenarians of 4.4 per 10,000 and life expectancy at 65 of 22.18 years or more. Each threshold is the population-weighted 75th percentile of land hexes: the value three in four residents live at or below. Touching hexes with all three make a zone, named after its most populous municipality: 60 zones, 347 hexes and 6,750,151 residents; the largest, Zamora (71), Ourense (53), Béjar (45), Segovia (30), Soria (13), Peñaranda de Bracamonte (13), Madrid (9), Burgo de Osma-Ciudad de Osma (9). They are mostly the Duero plateau and Ourense, plus the city of Madrid. In part this is depopulated Spain: 55% of the zones' hexes have fewer than 12.5 inhabitants per km² (the sparsely populated cut-off of the EU Guidelines on regional State aid, 2021/C 153/01), against 45% of land hexes, and 58% are in the quarter of hexes with the largest share of people over 65. Outside the 155 municipalities with a life expectancy of their own, the one at 65 is the province's, so where it decides, a zone's edge follows the province border. Annual Population Census of 2026 and life expectancy of 2024.

34.name: Standout offence
34.unit: offence type furthest above Spain's rate
34.note: Per resident: in tourist places (Benidorm, Marbella, Ibiza, Lloret de Mar…) visitors add offences but no Padrón residents. These are offences known to the police, not all that happen.
34.description: For each listed municipality or rest of a province, the offence type whose rate per inhabitant is the most times Spain's, among those with more than about 20,000 a year: theft, online fraud, burglary, violent robbery, assault, vehicle theft, drug trafficking, sexual offences and other cybercrime. It is painted only at 1.25 times Spain's rate or more and in units of 20,000 inhabitants or more (our cut-offs): below that, a few cases or a few percent would decide the colour. Left uncoloured for that reason: Cabra, El Hierro, Formentera and rest of Eivissa. Left out, as one or two cases would decide a town: homicides (376), attempted homicides (1,413) and kidnapping (109) in 2025; the rest of conventional crime is not a type. A hex takes the colour of the unit with most of its residents, the first in the tooltip, which gives each unit's type, its rate and how many times Spain's it is. It measures which offence stands out, not how much there is: a quiet place can stand out in cybercrime or burglary with a low total rate. Criminal offences known to the Policía Nacional, the Guardia Civil, the regional police forces and the local ones that report to the Sistema Estadístico de Criminalidad, by complaint or by the police's own action (Ministerio del Interior, Balance de Criminalidad, January to December 2025). The 427 municipalities the balance lists (those over 20,000 inhabitants by its reference padrón) have their own rate; Ceuta and Melilla appear as cities, with the rate of the whole city. Every other municipality takes the rate of the rest of its province (in the Balearic and Canary Islands, of its island): its offences and residents minus those of the listed municipalities.

35.name: Iberian lynx
35.unit: of the hex in squares where it was reported
35.note: 10 km squares reported to the EU for 2013-2018 (Habitats Directive, Art. 17). The 2025 census counts 2,269 individuals. An empty square does not prove the species is absent.
35.description: The 2025 census counts 2,269 individuals in 6 communities; the 2013-2018 squares do not reach Region of Murcia, Castile and León or Community of Madrid. They are Andalusia, Castilla–La Mancha, Extremadura, Region of Murcia, Castile and León and Community of Madrid. Each hex shows how much of it lies inside the 145 squares of 10 km where Spain reported the Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) to the European Union for 2013-2018, in the report under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive. The squares are those of the European reference grid (ETRS89-LAEA), from the Banco de Datos de la Naturaleza of the Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico; the part is measured at 84 points per hex, 1 km apart. A square places the species somewhere in its 100 km² and does not locate dens or nests; the ministry's files mark none of these records as sensitive. An empty square may not have been surveyed, or its community may not have reported it.
